A1.justification: Both PDFs describe T2AV-Compass and its 500-prompt benchmark. The complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures, equations, and embedded prompt templates, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 11 audiovisual generation systems in Tables 2–3, with detailed scores and model analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports evaluations of 15 systems and adds original human-agreement, robustness, sensitivity, and calibration results.

M1.justification: The objective evaluator adds NISQA speech-quality scoring and combines PQ and CU into Audio Aesthetics. The central prompt-construction and reasoning-first Gemini judging procedures remain unchanged; the complete prompt appendix is retained.

E1.justification: The 500-prompt suite, comprising 400 rewritten and 100 video-inverted prompts, retains its domains and tasks. The new human studies use validation subsets, and the real-video calibration concerns reference material already described in v1 Appendix F.2; these do not establish new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 expand from 11 to 15 systems by adding LTX-2, HunyuanVideo1.5 + Hunyuan-Foley, Wan-2.2 + MMAudio, and HunyuanVideo1.5 + MMAudio. New judge comparisons evaluate Gemini-2.5-Flash and Qwen3-Omni alongside Gemini-2.5-Pro. The sub-dimension plots also change their selected comparator set.

E3.justification: The objective metrics replace separate PQ/CU reporting with AA and add NISQA speech quality. New protocols include five-annotator studies on 50 prompts across five systems, forced-choice pairwise comparisons, and controlled preprocessing tests on 100 videos. Existing generation configurations and default judge settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's sub-dimension comparisons, v2 adds complexity-dependent failure analysis, audio-error decomposition, human validation of judging and synchronization, preprocessing sensitivity, metric-redundancy analysis, real-video calibration, and two qualitative case studies. These substantially expand evidence about benchmark reliability and failure mechanisms.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports three judging runs on the same 500 videos with coefficient-of-variation statistics, agreement standard deviations and sample counts, human/judge correlations, and Bradley–Terry estimation. v1 reports no comparable uncertainty or repeatability analysis. These additions do not establish repeated generation runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds four systems' scores and extensive validation and diagnostic outcomes. Most matched leaderboard values remain unchanged, but Table 3 revises Wan-2.2 + Hunyuan-Foley's IF Audio from 38.19 to 37.10 and Average from 58.40 to 58.13. Appendix C also replaces some existing speech-related scores with dashes; its percentage rescaling alone is not a result change.

T1.justification: Section 3.3.1 introduces the composite definition AA = (PQ + CU)/2, and Appendix D.5 adds mathematical specification of pairwise ranking and its Elo-style conversion. These are limited formal additions; neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the 500-prompt benchmark, unified objective and judge-based evaluation, and diagnosis of persistent realism and alignment failures. Evaluating 15 rather than 11 systems expands support without redefining these headline scientific claims.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies and expands interpretation: closed-source superiority becomes dimension-dependent, audio failures involve semantic matching and temporal control as well as physical grounding, and causal attribution is explicitly restrained. It adds limitations concerning proprietary-judge version drift, cautions against relying on aggregate rankings, and discusses judge weaknesses revealed by calibration.

D1.justification: Appendix E.1 newly documents score normalization, hierarchical IF aggregation, and the NonSpeech penalty and default. Section 3.1 adds curation counts and rewriting statistics. These clarify existing procedures; generation resolutions, judge decoding, frame sampling, synchronization settings, prompt templates, and code/data destinations are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for LTX-2, MMAudio, HunyuanVideo1.5, NISQA, and Bradley–Terry, replaces the LAION-5B citation with Aesthetic Predictor V2.5, and removes Flow-GRPO. Related work explicitly describes VABench as contemporaneous, while the broader research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: v2 condenses related work and method explanations, reorganizes the results discussion under diagnostic headings, improves cross-references and acronym consistency, and adds appendix sections. The main section sequence and full prompt-template text remain largely intact; much of the expansion is new scientific content.

P2.justification: The visual presentation is substantially revised: the overview moves to page 1, the original dataset figure is split, comparison plots are redesigned, and new failure curves, agreement tables, a correlation heatmap, calibration bars, and qualitative panels appear. The appendix complexity chart redisplays existing data rather than adding coverage.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of empirical validation for its central automated judge through human comparisons, repeatability checks, sensitivity tests, and calibration, while making score aggregation reproducible. These gains strengthen the benchmark's evidential foundation. New reporting errors require correction: Appendix D.5's Elo probability interpretation conflicts with its equations, and its claim that JavisDiT wins below 2% against every opponent contradicts Table 9. These localized problems do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.
